analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour over five years and ends lower minimum wages for tipped, teen, and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The Senate's $15 minimum wage bill, with 32 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the federal minimum wage in yearly steps from $8.55 to $15.00 an hour, then tied future increases to the growth in typical wages so the minimum does not lose value again. It also would have eliminated the special lower minimum wages for tipped workers, newly hired workers under 20, and workers with disabilities, eventually paying all of them the full minimum. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly the lowest-paid workers in the country: everyone earning between the $7.25 federal minimum and the new higher rates, disproportionately adults in their prime working years in service jobs. Tipped workers, teen hires, and workers with disabilities paid subminimum wages would eventually earn the same floor as everyone else. Workers who keep jobs would see direct raises year after year.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $8.55 to $15.00 an hour over five years, then indexes it to the growth in the median hourly wage so it does not erode again.
It phases out the lower 'tipped minimum wage' so tipped workers must eventually be paid the full federal minimum by their employer, while guaranteeing they keep all tips they receive.
It eliminates the lower youth minimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 after a transition period, so young workers are paid the same as everyone else.
It ends the practice of paying workers with disabilities subminimum wages, phasing them up to the full minimum wage and sunsetting the special certificates that allowed subminimum pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay wages near the minimum, especially small businesses, restaurants, and labor-intensive service companies, would bear higher payroll costs. Consumers would pay some of it in prices, and the bill's critics argue some marginal jobs would be eliminated or automated.

drawbacks.text: Opponents of minimum wage increases argue that sharply raising employer costs can lead to job losses, reduced hours, or automation, particularly for small businesses in low-wage regions — a concern heightened by a near-doubling of the federal wage floor in five years.

The bill eliminates the separate lower minimum wage for tipped employees; restaurant owners argued this would pressure restaurant finances, though the bill lets workers keep all their tips and phases the change in.

Eliminating subminimum wage certificates for workers with disabilities raises the risk that some sheltered employers would end jobs rather than pay full wages; the bill responds by requiring the Labor Department to help employers transition and to connect workers with competitive employment options, but the transition risk was real and widely acknowledged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and well-documented in the bill's own terms: a $7.25 wage is the longest the federal floor has gone without an increase since it was created, and the bill raised it substantially for the lowest-paid workers while phasing in over five years and indexing afterward. The real costs fall on small employers with thin margins, especially in low-cost regions, and some economists warn of job losses or reduced hours; the bill's phase-in and small transition assistance for disability employers mitigate but do not eliminate that risk. Ending the tipped and disability subminimum wages was the most contested design choice — supporters call it a pay equity fix; the restaurant industry called it a threat to a business model — and honest supporters acknowledge the transition risk for workers in those settings.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate committee that handles labor law, and that committee never took it up, so it sat and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the bill on January 16, 2019, with a group of Democratic senators including Schumer, Murray, and Warren.
Thirty-two Democratic senators signed on as cosponsors, but no Republicans did.
The Senate's only action was to read it twice and refer it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers paying around the federal minimum wage, especially in restaurants and retail, kept the existing lower wage floor. Workers earning $7.25 an hour gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers; tipped-wage restaurant model intact

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 32 Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: 32 Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors, including Chuck Schumer and Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the Senate's Democratic leader was among them.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought a minimum wage increase to the Senate floor in the 116th Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-run committee to which it was referred took no action.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill raises the wage floor for a heavily minimum-wage industry and eliminates the separate tipped minimum wage, requiring employers to pay the full minimum as cash wages. Restaurant chains that rely on the tipped wage would bear the direct cost.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops employing workers with disabilities
industries.note: The bill ends special certificates allowing subminimum pay to workers with disabilities and phases those wages up to the full minimum, with transition assistance. Programs built on subminimum pay would have to change their business model.

industries.industry: Low-wage retail, hospitality, and other large employers of minimum-wage workers
industries.note: Any employer paying near $7.25 would see labor costs rise on a fixed schedule. Large chains with thin-margin, high-turnover staffing bear the largest payroll increases.

industries.industry: Wealthier households and shareholders of labor-intensive companies
industries.note: Higher wage bills generally come out of profits, prices, or headcount; shareholders of firms dependent on minimum-wage labor would absorb part of the cost.
